cards.claim: Convergence bounds tighten when learning rate is small, momentum and batch size are large
cards.conditions: Muon optimizer without weight decay, L-smooth loss, standard SGD assumptions
cards.effect: Tighter convergence guarantees (upper bound on gradient norm decreases)
cards.quote: Theorem 3.1 suggests that setting the learning rate small and the momentum and batch size large results in a tighter bounds.

cards.claim: For Muon with weight decay to converge, learning rate and weight decay coefficient must satisfy λ·lr ≤ L
cards.conditions: Muon with decoupled weight decay and momentum, L-smooth losses
cards.effect: Convergence requirement; constrains valid hyperparameter combinations
cards.quote: the learning rate and weight decay coefficient must satisfy , a condition supported by our experimental results (see Figure 1 )

cards.claim: Weight decay ensures almost-sure boundedness of parameter and gradient norms without assuming bounded gradients
cards.conditions: Muon with weight decay (λ·lr ≤ L), L-smooth loss, λ small relative to gradient scale
cards.quote: We prove that incorporating weight decay ensures almost-sure boundedness of both the parameter and gradient norms (Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 ) without assuming bounded gradients

cards.claim: Convergence depends on effective rank of gradients, not full parameter dimension
cards.conditions: Muon algorithm, neural network gradients with low-rank structure, overparameterized regime
cards.effect: Variance term scales with effective rank r_g rather than full dimension d; can reduce variance scaling by factor up to d/r_g
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1), empirical measurement on FashionMNIST MLP (Appendix I)
cards.quote: The distinguishing feature of Muon's bound lies in the variance term , which depends on the rank rather than the full dimension . In practical deep networks, the effective rank of gradient matrices is often much smaller than the full dimension (i.e., ), particularly in over-parameterized regimes where gradients exhibit low-rank structure.

cards.claim: Critical batch size exists as a global minimizer that balances convergence steps vs batch size for SFO complexity minimization
cards.conditions: Muon with any of four variants (±Nesterov ±weight decay), convex convergence step function in batch size
cards.effect: SFO complexity has a well-defined minimum; beyond critical batch size, increasing batch size gives diminishing returns in step reduction
cards.evidence: Theoretical proof (Proposition 4.2) showing critical batch size is global minimum of C_SFO(B)=B·S(ε,B)
cards.quote: The critical batch size is therefore the batch size that minimizes SFO complexity . Prior work has shown that depends on both the optimizer ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) and dataset size ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and has established a theoretical framework for proving its existence and estimating its lower bound

cards.claim: Critical batch size lower bound depends on momentum, weight decay, gradient variance, effective rank, and target precision
cards.conditions: Muon with Nesterov momentum and weight decay (most practical variant), λ·lr ≤ L, λ·B_crit ≤ o(1)
cards.effect: B_crit scales with (1+β)², inversely with variance σ², inversely with effective rank r_M, inversely with target precision ε; depends on weight decay coefficient λ
cards.evidence: Theoretical derivation (Proposition 4.3, stated in abstract), SFO complexity minimization framework
cards.quote: we derive a lower bound on the critical batch size for the four Muon variants (Proposition 4.3 ). cards.claim: Newton-Schulz approximation error decays exponentially with iteration count and has negligible practical impact
cards.conditions: Muon with Newton-Schulz iterations (practical implementation), fixed number of iterations k (typically ~5-10)
cards.effect: Additional ξ_NS-dependent error term in convergence bound; empirical accuracy gain ≤ 0.5 pp vs SVD
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.3); empirical validation on ResNet widths (Appendix Table 8)
cards.quote: Since decays exponentially with , it is small for the fixed number of Newton-Schulz iterations used in practice, and its impact is therefore limited. In fact, according to Shen et al. (2025) , the experimental performance of the SVD-based Muon is equivalent to that of the Newton-Schulz-based version, with the main difference being the higher computational cost of the SVD procedure.

cards.claim: Weight decay improves convergence speed empirically through implicit regularization, not through tighter asymptotic rate
cards.conditions: Muon with weight decay (λ·lr ≤ L), training convergence curves
cards.effect: Faster empirical convergence observed; same asymptotic rate as without weight decay; benefit is implicit regularization of norms, not O(·) prefactor
